Adult individuals of the goatfish Upeneus pori attain a maximum fork length of 19 centimeters [Li = 19 centimeters], a value documented from extensive trawl surveys conducted throughout the eastern Mediterranean. In terms of body mass, the largest spawning adults reach an ultimate wet weight of 74.4 grams [Wwi = 74.4 grams], a figure derived from length–weight regressions and consistent with the moderate body plan typical of the Mullidae family. The growth trajectory linking length to mass in this small, demersal teleost follows a conventional allometric scaling relationship where wet weight increases as a power function of fork length, placing U. pori among the smaller-bodied members of its genus in the Levantine basin. Field records from the Israeli shelf indicate that specimens exceeding this length are uncommon, suggesting that the population experiences size-selective pressures from fishing operations. The maximum fork length represents a useful benchmark for comparing somatic investment across populations and is routinely incorporated into demographic models to estimate productivity. The consistency of these asymptotic values across multiple sampling years suggests a stable growth regime in the local population.

Reproductive maturation in Upeneus pori occurs at a moderate body size relative to the species’ ultimate length. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both sexes, is attained at a fork length of 10.6 centimeters [Lp = 10.6 centimeters]. This value has been corroborated by histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected during the pre-spawning season. At this length, the corresponding somatic investment is reflected by a wet weight at puberty of 12.2 grams [Wwp = 12.2 grams], a value that aligns with the energetic demands of reaching reproductive competence in a warm-temperate ecosystem. The shift from somatic growth to reproductive allocation is not abrupt in this species, as individuals of intermediate size often exhibit asynchronous gonadal development. The condition factor of fish at the pubertal transition remains relatively high, indicating that energy reserves are partitioned efficiently. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Upeneus moluccensis show that U. pori matures at a slightly smaller size, a difference that may reflect contrasting thermal regimes or local resource availability in their respective habitats.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of its natural spawning grounds (19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]), female Upeneus pori are capable of producing an estimated 473.5 eggs per day [Ri = estimated 473.5 eggs per day], a figure derived from extrapolation of fecundity data in the closely related species Upeneus moluccensis. This rate corresponds to a clutch size of approximately 710 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 710 eggs per spawning event] and an average spawning frequency of roughly one event every 1.5 days [F_R_i = roughly one event every 1.5 days] during the peak reproductive season. These sub-expressions highlight the remarkable reproductive output of this small mulid, which compensates for its modest body size by producing numerous small, pelagic eggs annually. The thermal regime at 19.2 °C appears to represent an optimal temperature for vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation, as deviations from this value have been linked to reduced batch fecundity in field-collected individuals. The high daily rate underscores the species’ role as an important forage fish in the Levantine food web.

Neonatal life stages in Upeneus pori commence with the release of small, buoyant eggs into the water column where they undergo pelagic development. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from an egg with a diameter of approximately 1 millimeter, and the ensuing wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], a value typical of demersal-spawning teleosts that produce numerous offspring with minimal per-offspring investment. These tiny prolarvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching, with exogenous feeding commencing only after mouth opening and retinal differentiation have occurred. The low birth mass reflects a reproductive strategy that prioritizes fecundity over offspring size, a pattern common among species that broadcast spawn in unstable pelagic environments. Field surveys of ichthyoplankton suggest that the yolk-sac stage lasts approximately three to four days at the ambient temperatures of the Mediterranean summer, after which the larvae must successfully transition to active feeding to avoid starvation. The high larval mortality associated with this small initial size is offset by the considerable daily egg production of mature females, a trade-off central to the species’ life-history strategy.

Longevity in Upeneus pori has been inferred from length-frequency analysis and otolith readings of individuals collected across the species’ range. The maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days], equivalent to roughly five years when estimated from incremental growth zones at a temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. This value was recorded at the ambient thermal regime of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], a temperature that supports moderate growth rates and delayed senescence in this warm-water teleost. The lifespan of U. pori is notably shorter than that reported for some larger-bodied mullids, yet it is comparable to other small, fast-growing demersal fishes that experience high natural mortality rates from predation and fishing pressure. The combination of early maturation at 10.6 centimeters [Lp = 10.6 centimeters] and a moderate lifespan produces an average reproductive tenure of three to four years for a typical female. Population-level estimates of mortality derived from catch curves suggest that very few individuals survive beyond the fifth year, underscoring the short-lived nature of this species within the context of its ecological niche as a benthic invertivore.
